1.title: Know the words and the kinds of fitness centre
1.intro: A fitness centre helps people move more and stay safe. Start with the basic words and the places people train.
pts: Learn the terms: member, class, trainer, equipment, membership, waiver, drop-in, capacity.
Kinds of place: gym, studio, community recreation centre, sports league, outdoor club.
Name one member type in one line: age, goal, budget, free hours.
Visit three places and list what they offer and when they are busy.
Compare a membership, a class pack and a drop-in pass, and explain who each one suits.
Note which services are free, such as a public community centre drop-in, and which are paid.
List three needs a member may have: low cost, child care, a quiet time or a beginner class.
1.ex: A parent of two wants a 45-minute class at 6 p.m. near home. Your member profile says: weekday evenings, low cost, child-friendly. A drop-in costs 12 and a pack of 10 costs 90, so each class in the pack costs 90 / 10 = 9, which saves 3 per class.
1.act: Visit three places and fill a table of services, hours and price. Write one member profile.
1.std: Task: compare three places. Condition: by visit or public web page. Standard: table complete, profile fits one line.

2.title: Explain how a centre runs in one day
2.intro: Days follow a pattern. If you can describe it, you can plan staff, space and safety.
pts: A day has opening checks, front desk, classes, floor time, cleaning and closing checks.
Staff roles: front desk, trainer, instructor, cleaner, manager.
Capacity means the most people allowed in a room at once; stay under it.
Write a simple daily checklist for open and close.
Draw the path of one member: arrive, check in, change, train, clean up, leave.
Name the busiest hour and explain what extra staff or space it needs.
Describe how the front desk handles a late arrival, a lost item and a complaint.
2.ex: At 6 a.m. staff test the lights, check floors are dry, test the first aid kit and unlock. At 10 p.m. they count members out and lock up. If a room holds 20 and 26 people arrive for a 6 p.m. class, 26 - 20 = 6 must wait or join a later class.
2.act: Draw a one-day timeline for a small studio with roles and checks.
2.std: Task: make a day timeline. Condition: for a 150 m2 studio. Standard: each hour has a role and a check.

3.title: Plan and lead a safe basic session
3.intro: Now apply what you know. Plan a simple group session that is safe and clear.
pts: Every session has a warm-up, main part, cool-down and a short talk on safety.
Ask each person about injuries or health limits before they start.
Show an easy and a harder version of each move.
Use clear short cues and watch every person, not only the loudest.
Write the session plan with minutes for each part and check that they add up to the full time.
Demonstrate each move yourself, watch the group do it and correct one thing at a time.
Describe how to stop a session safely when someone feels dizzy or hurt.
3.ex: A 30-minute class: 5 minutes warm-up, 20 minutes circuit of 5 moves, 5 minutes stretch, and 5 + 20 + 5 = 30. Each move gets 20 / 5 = 4 minutes. Each move has a beginner option.
3.act: Plan and lead a 30-minute session for four friends. Write what you would change.
3.std: Task: lead a 30-minute session. Condition: with a written plan. Standard: all parts done, options shown, nobody left unsupervised.

4.title: Follow Canadian safety and legal rules
4.intro: Safety and law protect members and you. Learn which rules touch a centre.
pts: Staff usually need current first aid and CPR training; ask your insurer and province what is required.
Waivers and insurance help, but they do not remove your duty to keep people safe.
Playing recorded music in public can need a licence; check the current rules.
Building, fire, health and business rules are set by the city and province; check the current rule with the local authority.
List which records you must keep, such as incident reports and waivers, and for how long; check the provincial rule.
Find out whether your centre needs an emergency plan or a defibrillator; check the local rule.
Explain how accessibility rules affect doors, ramps and washrooms; check the current building rule.
4.ex: A member twists a knee. Staff stop the class, give first aid, call for help if needed and write an incident report the same day. The report lists the time, place, what happened, who helped and who was told. Staff then ask the insurer whether the injury must be reported.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten items.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unknowns say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price memberships and check it pays
5.intro: A centre needs enough members and classes to cover its costs. Work the numbers.
pts: Fixed costs: rent, insurance, utilities, wages, software. Variable costs: cleaning supplies, extra staff.
Break-even members = monthly fixed costs divided by profit per member.
Compare monthly, class-pack and drop-in prices.
Collect sales tax once registered; check the small-supplier limit with the tax agency.
Estimate monthly income as members times price, then subtract fixed and variable costs.
Test a price rise and recompute break-even.
Decide how many classes a week the room can hold and what each class must earn.
5.ex: Fixed costs are 9,000 dollars a month. Each member pays 55 and costs 5 to serve, so profit is 50, and break-even = 9,000 / 50 = 180 members. If the price rises to 60, profit is 55 and break-even is 9,000 / 55 = about 164 members. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Build a one-page budget and a break-even number for a small studio.
5.std: Task: compute break-even. Condition: with simple spreadsheet. Standard: every cost listed, formula shown, a mentor can follow it.

6.title: Attract members and keep them
6.intro: People join for a goal and stay for community. Plan how to be found and how to keep them.
pts: Offer a free trial class and ask how people heard about you.
Local ways to be found: community boards, schools, workplaces, a simple map listing.
Track visits per member; a member who stops visiting for three weeks needs a friendly message.
Get consent before sending marketing messages; follow Canada's anti-spam rules.
Ask three members what made them join and what would make them leave.
Make a welcome plan for a new member's first week: tour, intro class and one check-in message.
Count how many trial guests become members and write it as a percentage.
6.ex: A new member misses three weeks. You send: 'We saved your spot Tuesday. Want a free guest pass for a friend?' Of 10 trial guests, 4 join, so 4 / 10 = 40 percent became members.
6.act: Run a four-week trial offer for ten people and log who stays.
6.std: Task: run a trial offer. Condition: with consent for every message. Standard: ten people invited, results logged, one lesson written.

7.title: Protect people, data and equipment
7.intro: Care for people, their information and your gear is part of the job.
pts: Check equipment weekly: cables, bolts, mats, pins. Tag broken items out of use.
Keep health forms private and locked or password-protected.
Write rules for children, changing rooms and harassment. Staff must know how to report.
Clean shared equipment between uses and keep a cleaning log.
Post emergency steps and exits where staff and members can see them.
Train staff to report harassment or injury to a named person on the same day.
Create a spill and wet-floor routine and record each cleaning.
7.ex: A bench has a cracked pad. Staff tag it 'Out of use', record it, and order a repair the same day. If the weekly check covers 12 items and finds 2 faults, 2 / 12 is about 17 percent, so you re-check those items next week.
7.act: Write an equipment check list, an incident form and a code of conduct (one page each).
7.std: Task: write three safety documents. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each is clear, dated and has a named owner.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Test, measure and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day pilot goal, such as 30 members or 4 classes a week.
Every week record visits, income, costs, complaints and injuries.
Ask members for one thing to keep and one to change.
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
Define in advance what result means stop, change or grow.
Share the weekly numbers with your mentor and ask for one challenge.
Compare the real break-even with the planned one and explain the gap.
8.ex: After 60 days: 34 members, 1,870 dollars billed, 2 minor incidents with no injuries needing a doctor. 1,870 / 34 = 55 per member, which matches the price. You decide to add one evening class.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real members and agreed prices. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is a waiver?
A signed form where a member accepts known risks; it does not remove your duty to keep people safe.
What is capacity?
The most people allowed in a room at once.
What are the three parts of a safe session?
Warm-up, main part and cool-down.
Why ask members about injuries first?
To adjust moves and keep them safe.
How do you find break-even members?
Fixed costs divided by profit per member.
What training do staff usually need?
Current first aid and CPR; check what your insurer and province require.
What do you do with a broken machine?
Tag it out of use, record it and repair it.
When can you send marketing messages?
Only with consent, and with a way to unsubscribe.
Why keep health forms private?
They hold personal information protected by privacy law.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
